sources.title: Rifa'a at-Tahtawi (Q981929), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): label "Rifa'a at-Tahtawi", description 'Egyptian scholar (1801-1873)', born 15 October 1801, died 27 May 1873, no Korean label, image 'Tahtawi.jpg' (150 x 216). Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Rifaa et-Tahtavi', TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (Turkish Religious Foundation Encyclopedia of Islam), read in full in Turkish. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: presents him as an Egyptian scholar of language, literature, history and geography and a translator, who studied at al-Azhar (1817-21) under Hasan al-Attar, went to Paris in 1826 as imam of Muhammad Ali's student mission and wrote the Takhlis al-Ibriz about it, directed the School of Languages from 1835 (adding history, geography, mathematics and law to the curriculum; a preparatory school 1841, an accounting school 1845), edited the official gazette al-Waqa'i al-Misriyya from 1841, was sent by Abbas to Khartoum in 1850 to found a school there and returned in 1854, directed the military school 1856-60, and from 1863 headed the revived Translation Bureau and edited the journal Rawdat al-Madaris; lists his translations (geography, logic, geometry, the French Civil Code with a student, Fenelon's Telemaque) and his 1872 education treatise, and says efforts he supported led to a girls' school opened in January 1873. The entry is descriptive, gives no sustained critique, and ties his career closely to the rulers' changing patronage.

Jurji Zaydan, 'Rifa'a Bey Rafi' al-Tahtawi', in Tarajim Mashahir al-Sharq fi al-Qarn al-Tasi' 'Ashar, vol. 2, third edition (Cairo: Matba'at al-Hilal, 1922), Internet Archive scan from the Bibliotheca Alexandrina (item AAlexandrina-084569), pages 22-25 read as page images in Arabic: an early twentieth-century biography based, as Zaydan says, on Salih Majdi's manuscript biography of Tahtawi; gives his early life, Azhar teaching, appointment as imam of the 1241 AH mission to France, learning French at his own initiative, return in 1247, translation work at the medical, artillery and later other schools, the establishment of the gazette in 1248 AH with his help, the School of Languages opened in 1251 AH and entrusted to him (50 pupils at first, then 250), the Translation Bureau formed in 1258 AH, exile to Khartoum under Abbas I, the military school under Said, the abolition of the schools in 1277 AH and his return to the Translation Bureau and to editing Rawdat al-Madaris until his death in 1290 AH aged 75, and lists his works, noting that he translated one volume of Malte-Brun in sixty days and that the translation was hasty. Earlier-generation admiring biography relying on one manuscript source; the plate of his portrait in the same pages is the portrait review source.

Peter Gran, 'Tahtawi in Paris', a scholarly essay (open PDF hosted by Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Hitrade project), read in full: argues for a less Eurocentric reading, that his formation owed much to Tahta's culture and the Azhar curriculum rather than only to the French sojourn, that the 'dominant paradigm' leans on his exceptionalism, that his teacher Hasan al-Attar and he 'broke rank' with the Azhar by working for the government and were criticised for it, that his earnings in Paris (250 piasters) were a tenth of a less productive fellow student's (2500), that his mother objected to his going, and that the French loan words and ideas he introduced (citizens' rights, the Copernican view) were less of a rupture than usually claimed. Revisionist counter-voice; the essay is an essay rather than a full archival study and says some of its points are speculation.

Ines Ait Mokhtar, 'Tahtawi, le pionnier de la Nahda', Les cles du Moyen-Orient (French online magazine; published 2013, updated 2018), read in full in French: summary portrait: Azhar from 1817, Paris 1826-31, Takhlis al-Ibriz ('L'Or de Paris'), direction of the School of Languages and translations of French works (including Montesquieu on the Romans), publication of Arabic classics, exile to Khartoum under Abbas until 1854 where he translated Telemaque; notes he preferred an enlightened ruler to popular government (Hourani's 'conventional Islamic point of view'), criticised Azhar conservatism and was liberal toward Jews and Christians; warns that the 'nationalist' reading is an interpretation and that his political stance limits calling him a liberal. Popular-press synthesis with a short bibliography.

Abdallah Tagourramt El Kbaich, 'Al-Tahtawi en castellano', blog of the University of Barcelona project Cartografies literaries de la Mediterrania (27 November 2020), read in Spanish: review of the 2018 Spanish translation of the Takhlis al-Ibriz, describing its six essays (the journey to Marseille; Paris geography, customs, politics, education and the French Constitution; rhetoric and his relations with French orientalists; the 1830 revolution; the classification of French sciences and languages) and arguing that the book mirrors France to criticise Egypt and fits the adib ideal rather than the Azhar sheikh. Appreciative academic blog; no independent critical evaluation and no coverage of his school work.

Farah Rafik, 'How Rifa'a Al-Tahtawi pioneered the Egyptian intellectual awakening', Egyptian Streets (22 June 2022), read in full: laudatory popular article giving the career outline (Azhar at 17, Paris 1826, School of Languages, translation bureau) and quoting others calling him a pioneer of the Nahda, with the unsourced claim that he oversaw more than 2,000 translated books (not used). Used only for the dates it shares with the other sources.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_tahtawi_tdv, src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_calitme | 1821-1873 | encyclopedia entry, early twentieth-century biography, university review] The encyclopedia lists translations of geography (Malte-Brun), logic (Dumarsais), geometry (Legendre), the French Civil and Commercial Codes, Fenelon's Telemaque and a French verse lyric, alongside his own Arabic grammar in verse, a lexicon, a history of Egypt from the Pharaohs and a treatise on education; Zaydan's biography lists the same works and adds geography teaching books; the Spanish review describes the Takhlis as mixing memoir, poetry, history, geography, politics and jurisprudence and classifying French sciences. Breadth is documented by works and by posts across language, law, geography and military schools; the sources are admiring, but the lists are specific and agree. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): cross_domain_range lowered from 78 / 0.56 to 72 / 0.5 because the breadth is listed in an encyclopedia entry and an early biography; the assessments are descriptive and admiring, with one revisionist essay.

curiosity.rationale: [src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_tdv, src_tahtawi_calitme | 1826-1831 | early twentieth-century biography, encyclopedia entry, university review] Zaydan says that in Paris his own desire for Western learning led him to take up French by himself and then to study history, geography and other modern sciences, and the encyclopedia adds philosophy, mineralogy, mathematics, mythology and meetings with Jomard, Silvestre de Sacy and Caussin de Perceval; the Spanish review describes a Takhlis that surveys French politics, the 1830 revolution and the classification of sciences. Gran, the revisionist, argues the interest was already rooted in his Azhar and Tahta formation rather than created in Paris, which adjusts the story but not the existence of the interest. The behaviour is documented in several sources; the unprompted nature of it rests mainly on Zaydan, who relied on one manuscript source. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): curiosity lowered from 72 / 0.54 to 68 / 0.48 because curiosity is inferred from his Paris study and translation programme as described by institutional and biographical entries.

persistence.rationale: [src_tahtawi_tdv, src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_clefs | 1835-1873 | encyclopedia entry, early twentieth-century biography, press synthesis] The School of Languages that he ran from 1835 was closed in 1850 and he was sent to Khartoum, where the encyclopedia says he founded a school and completed several translations in four years; Zaydan says he stayed without a post from 1277 AH (1860) until he was put in charge of the Translation Bureau again and edited Rawdat al-Madaris until his death at 75; the French portrait says he translated Telemaque in Khartoum. He kept to educational and translation work through repeated closures, though the closures were the rulers' decisions and the evidence for his personal effort in the gaps is thin.

adaptability.rationale: [src_tahtawi_tdv, src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_gran, src_tahtawi_clefs | 1831-1863 | encyclopedia entry, early twentieth-century biography, revisionist essay, press synthesis] He moved between a medical school, an artillery school, the School of Languages, the Sudan school, the European Bureau, the military school and the Translation Bureau as different rulers (Muhammad Ali, Abbas, Said, Ismail) closed, reopened or reassigned institutions, and kept producing translations and teaching texts in each post; Gran notes that he and Hasan al-Attar 'broke rank' with the Azhar by working for the government and 'wisely simply distanced himself' from that milieu, and the French portrait notes that his political stance (an enlightened ruler rather than popular government) limits calling him a liberal reformer. The pattern is real flexibility, but also dependence on patronage; scored as dual-edged.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_tahtawi_tdv, src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_clefs | 1835-1873 | encyclopedia entry, early twentieth-century biography, press synthesis] The encyclopedia and Zaydan both list his 1872 treatise on the education of girls and boys written for a girls' school and say his efforts for girls' education contributed to a girls' school opening in January 1873; the encyclopedia credits him with enlarging the School of Languages' curriculum, and the French portrait calls him a theorist of education as the shaping of citizens. These document educational work, but no source assesses his intent and the evidence for the girls' school is a short mention in a descriptive entry. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.45 because the motive is inferred from descriptive and admiring entries only, the girls' school link is a one-line claim, and Gran's critique reads the reform movement as elitist.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_tahtawi_zaydan, src_tahtawi_tdv | 1830-1873 | early twentieth-century biography, encyclopedia entry] Zaydan says one large volume of Malte-Brun's geography was translated by him in sixty days in 1265 AH and adds that it appears to have been done in haste; the encyclopedia lists more than a dozen translations plus editorial work over four decades, including a volume in 1834 translated during six months in Tahta. A high pace of output is documented, with the biographer's own note that the speed cost polish; the figure rests on one early biography.

portrait.source: Anonymous drawing of Rifa'a al-Tahtawi in Arab dress, artist and date unknown. The same drawing is printed as plate 3 (captioned 'Rifa'a Bey Rafi' al-Tahtawi') in Jurji Zaydan's Tarajim Mashahir al-Sharq, volume 2, third edition (Cairo: Matba'at al-Hilal, 1922), Internet Archive scan from the Bibliotheca Alexandrina (item AAlexandrina-084569), where the text calls it his portrait; that 1922 print is the verified publication basis. The file is the clearer Wikimedia Commons scan of the same drawing ('Rifa'a el-Tahtawi.png', which its uploader attributes to a 1912 edition of his Manahij al-Albab), converted to JPEG on a white background at its original 758 x 877 pixels, not upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain (anonymous drawing published in 1922, before 1931)
portrait.attribution: Anonymous, portrait drawing of Rifa'a al-Tahtawi, printed in Jurji Zaydan, Tarajim Mashahir al-Sharq vol. 2 (Cairo, 1922); public domain

provenance.notes:
portrait_preflight: RISKY (alt-dependent) (lead) / RESOLVED via a replacement path: the lead's tiny en-wiki upload (Tahtawi.jpg, 150 x 216, uploader Zerida, tagged PD-Egypt with no source) was not used. The Wikimedia Commons file 'Rifa'a el-Tahtawi.png' (758 x 877) is a scan of a drawing of him that its page says comes from the second edition (1912) of his Manahij al-Albab; I could not open that edition, so the 1912 claim is the uploader's and is not relied on. The rights basis rests instead on a source I opened myself: the same drawing is printed as plate 3, captioned 'Rifa'a Bey Rafi' al-Tahtawi', in Jurji Zaydan's Tarajim Mashahir al-Sharq vol. 2, third edition, Matba'at al-Hilal, Cairo, 1922, Internet Archive item AAlexandrina-084569 (Bibliotheca Alexandrina scan), page 23 (I viewed the page image and compared the turban, face, cloak and sword hilt with the Commons image: the same drawing), and Zaydan's text says 'as you see in his portrait at the head of this article' and that he wore Arab dress until he returned from France. A work published in 1922 is public domain in the United States (published before 1931), and the drawing's artist is unknown, so the only unresolved facts are who drew it and when (undated, no later than 1922); the author of the text, Zaydan, died in 1914. The al-Zirikli 1958 plate (Commons 'Rifa'a el-Tahtawi - Al-Alam, V3, P 62.jpg', 1136 x 1492) is the same drawing but is a 1958 reproduction and was not used. The file used is the 758 x 877 Commons scan converted from PNG to JPEG over a white background, not upscaled. Kind historical_depiction because artist, date and sitting are undocumented. Honest caveat: the artist and the exact first publication are unknown; the basis is publication before 1931 of an anonymous drawing , verified in the 1922 Zaydan plate.

CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: 'Rifaa et-Tahtavi', TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/rifaa-et-tahtavi); Britannica was blocked (403).
READ: TDV entry (Turkish, in full), Zaydan's 1922 biography (Arabic page images 22-25), Gran's 'Tahtawi in Paris' (full), Les cles du Moyen-Orient portrait (French), the University of Barcelona CALITME review (Spanish), Egyptian Streets (English): six sources in four languages. PERSPECTIVES: encyclopedia, early twentieth-century biography relying on one manuscript, revisionist scholarly essay, press synthesis, university review, popular press. COUNTER-VOICES: Gran (the paradigm's exceptionalism, the Azhar's view of reformers as betrayers, unequal pay), and the French portrait (political limits). NOT OPENED: Hourani's Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age and Mitchell's Colonising Egypt (known only through the French portrait's and a search summary), Newman's An Imam in Paris, Salih Majdi's manuscript, the Takhlis itself, Britannica, Heyworth-Dunne. EXCLUDED: ranks and land grants, patriotic odes, the 1830 revolution's political lessons, family life. DATE CONFLICTS NOTED: sources differ on whether the School of Languages was founded in 1835 (TDV, renamed), 1836 (Egyptian Streets), or opened in 1251 AH, about 1835 (Zaydan); the cards use 'from 1835' with the encyclopedia.
MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT SELF-GATE: first pass PASS on all five checks (see draft review).
SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): rows reviewed: impact_motivation (lowered 68 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.45: motive inferred from descriptive and admiring entries), cross_domain_range (kept: documented list of works and posts in several sources), curiosity (kept: several sources, adjusted by Gran's caution). BROAD FLAG: the evidence for his personality is mostly institutional and bibliographic; a later pass reading Hourani's chapter, Newman's introduction or Majdi would strengthen the behavioural rows.
